case_data.title: We the Internet
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
**We, the Internet was the first deliberative citizens' dialogue on internet governance and AI held at a global scale. In its 2020 edition, coordinated by Missions Publiques, it engaged more than 5,500 citizens across 75+ countries in a single structured "Deliberation Day," alongside a separate global Stakeholders' Dialogue of 340+ participants. **

Randomly selected citizens were given balanced information materials and then deliberated in facilitated small groups on four themes: digital identity and data, the digital public sphere and disinformation, governing artificial intelligence, and internet governance. The dedicated AI session was designed to surface how ordinary people — not experts — want AI to be governed. Results were synthesised into key messages and channelled to decision-makers, feeding into the UN Secretary-General's Roadmap on Digital Cooperation, and later the Global Digital Compact.
case_data.what-limitations-to-the-project-should-b: COVID-19 disrupted delivery — many planned in-person dialogues moved online, and some partners and would-be participants could not take part in time, affecting country coverage.
case_data.headline-findings:
Citizens worldwide said AI is "a powerful tool that needs careful stewardship" — rejecting both naïve enthusiasm and catastrophism.

Citizens said their own understanding of AI was not high enough for a fully informed debate — and judged that companies and governments face the same gap — yet still wanted the conversation pursued.
Citizens set two clear priorities for AI: it should be used for the common good, and its governance should be designed so that no one is left out.
On disinformation, citizens ranked education as the most urgent and effective remedy, ahead of human content moderation and legal regulation; voluntary self-commitments by companies had the least support.
On data, citizens said a data-driven society could be positive only under conditions — data tied to human rights, trustworthy, controllable and accessible by citizens, and governed in a science-based, multistakeholder way.
Across all themes, citizens strongly backed multistakeholder, global, science-based governance — and saw citizen deliberation itself as a crucial instrument.
Views converged remarkably across regions: participants from North and South, East and West reached very similar positions, suggesting a shared global public vision.
case_data.inclusion-efforts:
Recruitment criteria explicitly included "connectedness," so partners reached non-connected and low-connectivity citizens, not only habitual internet users. National partners could add criteria of national relevance, such as ethnic or religious groups, to reach minorities. 

No prior knowledge was required: each session opened with plain-language videos and balanced texts so anyone could form an informed view, and trained facilitators ensured every person in a group spoke. Materials were produced in multiple languages, dialogues ran both face-to-face and online, and food and refreshments were provided free to in-person participants.
case_data.why-is-this-project-important-to-include: It is one of the earliest and largest attempts to put AI governance directly to a globally representative public rather than to experts. Three things stand out: (1) genuinely global reach with striking cross-cultural convergence — citizens from the global North and South, East and West reached very similar conclusions; (2) deliberate inclusion of non-connected citizens and minorities, not just typical "online" populations; and (3) a reusable, openly licensed method — balanced information materials, facilitation scripts and questionnaires — published as a toolkit so any country can run its own dialogue. The AI session itself was co-designed with academic research on participatory AI governance methods.
project-goals: Methods: Create re-usable participation tools & methods
Quantitative: Generate statistical evidence on public attitudes to AI
Qualitative: Capture qualitative evidence on public attitudes to AI
Capacity: Build participant capacity to engage with AI
Empowerment: Build community power with respect to AI
case_data.describe-the-subject-matter-in-your-own-: How ordinary citizens worldwide want artificial intelligence — and the wider internet — to be governed
